title: Vegetables

learn.summary: Most people who think they hate vegetables have only had them steamed to gray or boiled to mush. High heat is the great converter: roasting and sautéing caramelize natural sugars and create textures worth craving. The skills here — high-heat roasting, a proper sauté, blanching, and confident raw prep — turn the produce drawer from obligation into the best part of the plate.

do: Roast any vegetable at 425°F tonight — oiled, salted, single layer — and pull it only when the edges are deeply browned

children.title: Roasting

learn.summary: The formula: 400-450°F, vegetables cut evenly, tossed in enough oil to gleam, salted, and spread in a single layer with space between pieces — crowding steams, space browns. Do not stir for the first 15-20 minutes so the cut sides caramelize against the hot pan. Dense roots take 30-45 minutes; broccoli and cauliflower 20-25.

do: Roast broccoli at 425°F for 22 minutes without stirring once, and serve it with lemon squeezed over — compare it to any steamed broccoli memory

children.title: Sautéing

learn.summary: Sauté means jump: high heat, a little fat, food in a single layer, kept moving just enough to brown without burning. The pan must be hot before the food goes in, and the food must be dry — wet greens spit and steam. Aromatics have an order: onions first (5-8 minutes), garlic last (30-60 seconds), because garlic burns bitter fast.

do: Sauté zucchini or green beans over confident high heat this week: hot pan, shimmering oil, single layer, and toss only every 60-90 seconds

children.title: Blanching & Shocking

learn.summary: Blanching — a brief plunge into heavily salted boiling water, then straight into ice water — sets vivid color and crisp-tender texture, and it is the restaurant secret behind perfect green vegetables. Green beans take 2-3 minutes, broccoli 2, peas 1. Shocked vegetables hold in the fridge for days, ready for a 90-second reheat in butter or a cold salad.

do: Blanch and shock a batch of green beans on Sunday (2.5 minutes, then ice water), stash them in the fridge, and reheat portions in butter on two weeknights

children.title: Raw & Salads

learn.summary: A great salad is engineering: bone-dry leaves (dressing slides off wet ones — a salad spinner earns its space), dressing added in stages and tossed with your hands, and seasoning like any other dish — salt on the leaves, not just in the vinaigrette. The classic vinaigrette ratio is 3 parts oil to 1 part acid, adjusted to taste, with mustard to help it hold together. Dress at the last minute; acid wilts greens fast.

do: Make a 3:1 vinaigrette in a jar this week (6 tbsp olive oil, 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp mustard, salt), shake, and dress properly dried greens with your hands
